text:
Every test passes. Two dashboards report revenue for the same twelve orders. One says nineteen hundred forty-nine dollars. The other says forty-five hundred fifty-five. Neither query errors, and neither looks wrong. Interviews probe exactly this: who defines a number, and the joins that quietly change it. Eighteen questions on metrics and the semantic layer. Eight are worked through, most on the page's own orders in Postgres, and ten come quickly at the end.

Question one. What causes two dashboards to report different numbers for the same metric? Two hand-written definitions. One counts refunds, tax or cancelled orders, and the other doesn't. One goes by order date, the other by ship date. They aggregate at different grains. Or one of them hits a fan trap. Here, it's the fan trap. The cure is one shared definition, in a semantic layer or a certified mart, so both dashboards run identical sequel. Left alone, the gap grows: each definition weighs a shift in traffic differently, so they drift apart just when everyone is looking.

Question two. What is a fan-out join, or fan trap, and why is it dangerous? You join a table to a one-to-many detail table, then sum a measure from the one side. Orders one and two are worth a hundred fifty dollars. Order one has three items, order two has one. Join the items, and order one's hundred dollars appears three times: three hundred fifty. Across all twelve orders, the join returns twenty-four rows, and nineteen hundred forty-nine dollars becomes forty-five hundred fifty-five, more than double. That's the danger: nothing errors, and the result looks ordinary. Each order is counted once per item, so the bigger the baskets, the bigger the error. The tell is the row count. Twelve orders went into the join, and twenty-four rows came out.
